tagline.text: A deep wall dive site off northern Boracay for advanced divers only

location.label: Location
location.text: Waters off Yapak, northern Boracay Island, Malay, Aklan

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: About 45 minutes underwater (half a day including the boat)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱2,400~5,000 (boat dive from about ₱2,400; whether gear and a second dive are included depends on the operator)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Caticlan Airport (MPH, Godofredo P. Ramos Airport) or Kalibo International Airport (KLO)

children.text: Yapak is a dive site off northern Boracay, known for walls that start at about 30 m and drop beyond 60 m, and for strong currents. Large fish such as barracuda, trevally, tuna and whitetip reef sharks can be seen, so advanced divers seek it out, but with little experience the currents and depth make it dangerous.

Yapak is a dive site in the sea north of Boracay Island. It is known as a deep site with strong currents among Boracay's 25-plus dive points, and most guides classify it as for advanced divers and above. Depth figures differ a little between guides, but the most common description is a wall that starts around 30 m and continues to 60 m or deeper, and some listings give a maximum of about 70 m. According to dive operators the site is divided into several sections such as Yapak 1 and Yapak 2, and the entry point changes with the current of the day.

Underwater the scenery is walls covered in coral and large sea fans (gorgonians) and open blue water. One site description rated visibility at 30 m or more, and barracuda, tuna, giant trevally, whitetip reef sharks, grey reef sharks and dogtooth tuna are mentioned often. Some guides say hammerheads and manta rays are very occasionally seen, but this is not guaranteed. Near Yapak on the east side there is also a cave point called Bat Cave, which you should not enter when the sea and currents are rough.

This is not a site for everybody. Some operators require more than an Advanced Open Water certification, such as a certain number of logged dives and deep and drift experience. One operator states that it requires Advanced Open Water, 30 or more logged dives, deep and drift experience and an assessment dive. That is one operator's standard, not a universal rule; other guides likewise present Yapak only as a drift site suited to Advanced Open Water divers and above, and the required number of logged dives varies by operator, so confirm before diving. The same source warns that you should not assume an Advanced card alone qualifies you for a 40 m dive.

This guide is not an instruction for beginners or uncertified people to follow; it is an overview to help advanced divers planning to dive in Boracay understand Yapak. Dive prices, boat times and entry methods vary with the operator and the weather, so I have given ranges and marked them "check locally". Enter the water only with an operator and guide suited to your certification. Boracay has dozens of dive centers along White Beach and more than 25 dive points. If you are a beginner or uncertified, start with a shallow, gentle site or a discovery dive, and take on a site like Yapak only after earning an advanced certification and building up your logbook. For example, Friday's Rock off Balabag on the west coast is described as having a fish-feeding area and is far less demanding than Yapak.

The wall starts at about 30 m and continues beyond 60 m. Some listings give a maximum of about 70 m. For most recreational divers this depth is beyond their limits, so proper certification and gas planning are essential.
Barracuda, tuna, trevally, whitetip reef sharks and grey reef sharks are the typical sightings. There are occasional reports of hammerheads or manta rays, but they depend on luck.
Yapak 2 is described as having coral and large sea fans covering the wall. On clear days a big blue view opens out toward open water.

The strong current often makes it a drift dive. One listing gives the current speed as about 2 knots. On some days the water moves so fast that photography is difficult, so the guide decides the entry method based on conditions that day. On days when the current is weak the dive is easier than usual, but never be careless.
A cave point on the east side of the north end, where lobsters, sea snakes and small tropical fish are reported. It is a challenging place to enter only in the best conditions.

Punta Bunga on the Balabag side of the west coast has a shallow wall down to about 24 m and a deep wall at 30–50 m, so it is gentler than Yapak. If Yapak feels like too much, it is safer to plan your dives at other Boracay points.
You can dive Boracay all year, but visibility is best from October to May, especially April to June. Guides say currents are stronger and visibility slightly lower from December to February.

items.title: A diving day
items.subtitle: Half a day by operator boat

children.text: Meet the operator's staff at your lodging, check your gear and listen to the dive briefing.
Board the dive boat at the boarding point set by the operator and head to the waters off Yapak in the north. The boarding place and travel time depend on the operator and the weather.
Explore the Yapak wall on your first dive. It lasts about
45 minutes
and the entry method is set by the guide's judgment of the current.
During the surface interval, have a snack and confirm the plan for the second dive.
Depending on conditions, the second dive may be switched to a shallower site.
Return to port, put your gear away and get your dive log signed.
After diving you must rest enough before flying. The general recommendation is 18 hours or more, so schedule flights after your last dive and check the operator's and your dive insurance's rules.
The flight from Manila to Caticlan Airport (MPH) takes about
1 hour
. From the airport to the Caticlan jetty port is about
3 minutes
by tricycle.
Fares into Kalibo International Airport (KLO) tend to be cheaper, but from Kalibo it is another
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours
by van or bus to the Caticlan jetty port.
Flight schedules and fares change with the season and airline, so check before booking.

items.title: From the island to the dive boat

children.text: Most dive operators are on the beach around Stations 1–3 of White Beach. Operators often help with lodging pickup and transfer to the boat, so check when you book.
Yapak is in the north of Boracay, so you go by boat from the beach. Boat travel time varies with the current and waves, so check locally.
If you will dive several days in a row, decide in advance how to carry your heavy gear bag from the airport to your lodging. Ask for an electric tricycle or lodging pickup to make it easier.

You can dive Boracay all year, but Yapak has strong currents, so you need to pay attention to weather and season. One guide says visibility is good from October to May and clearest in April to June, adding that from December to February the current is stronger and visibility may be slightly lower.
The water temperature averages about
and is said to rarely fall below
. Whether you can actually enter the water is decided by the operator and guide based on the current and waves that day.

Conditions at Yapak are not the same at the same time every year. Even within a month the difference between weak-current and strong-current days is large, so it is common to plan several days and dive on the most stable one. When you book, be sure to check the cancellation and rescheduling terms.

In Boracay, lodging around Stations 1–3 of White Beach is close to the dive operators, which makes getting around easy. Yapak dives often leave early in the morning, so it is better to choose lodging near the beach that fits an early start.

Some operators provide snacks and water on the boat during the rest between dives; check whether they are included when you book. For a meal after diving, the restaurants around D'Mall give you plenty of choice. Avoid alcohol the night before diving and leave plenty of time after diving before you drink.

If you dive several days in a row, check that your lodging has space to dry your gear and a shower. On rest days you can go to Puka Beach for a light swim. Between dives, bring plenty of water and simple snacks to replenish fluids and salt.
Bring your certification card (Advanced or above), logbook and recent dive records, and be honest with the operator about your experience.
In the guide's briefing, be sure to confirm the entry method, current direction, ascent method and emergency signals.
Bring an SMB (surface marker buoy) and a dive computer, and do not leave the guide's side on drift dives.
You may see big fish, but it is not guaranteed. Keep your expectations low and put safety first.
Do not fly after diving; leave plenty of rest time. The usual recommendation is 18 hours or more.
If Yapak feels like too much, switching your plan to a gentler point such as Punta Bunga is the wise choice.
Even with water at about 28℃ you can feel cold at depth, so consider a wetsuit of at least 3 mm.
Dives can be cancelled because of weather and current, so allow at least one spare day.
The night before diving, avoid late nights, overeating and heavy drinking, and sleep well.
Ask the operator whether they accept card payment as well as cash. Boracay has ATMs, but the lines can be long.
Yapak needs advanced certification and plenty of experience because of its deep walls below 30 m and strong currents. If you are not certified, do not enter the water.
One listing says the current can reach about 2 knots, so there is a risk of divers being separated. Always carry an SMB and signaling gear.
At depth the risk of decompression sickness rises. Keep strictly to your dive plan and flying times.
Do not dive if you are unwell or have a cold or ear problem.
Enter the cave point (Bat Cave) only in good conditions, and non-specialists should not approach it.
Prices and whether the site can be dived depend on the operator and the weather.
Do not force yourself to fit Yapak. If your condition or the conditions do not match, switching to another point is the best safety rule.
